changed_views: Enterprise AI spend is escaping the IT budget and becoming a line-of-business compute allocation problem.
Per-seat SaaS pricing is unlikely to survive unchanged when agents become high-volume headless users of enterprise data.
follow_ups: Track whether enterprise SaaS vendors disclose agent or consumption pricing separate from seats.
Watch for tooling that measures ROI per token across line-of-business budgets.

signals.claim: Levie says token budgeting is now one of the hottest enterprise AI issues because agent economics broke $20-seat assumptions.
signals.evidence: He says larger contexts, bigger models, and better agents mean one task can consume about $1,000 of compute, which cannot fit into chatbot or Copilot-style seat pricing.

signals.claim: Levie says frontier-token prices are not falling like normal compute because the industry compressed a decade of rollout into roughly 12-18 months.
signals.evidence: He argues bigger models, hardware scarcity, capacity constraints, and lab/provider pricing power have delayed the usual scale-driven cost declines.

signals.claim: Levie says AI spend will move from IT budgets into line-of-business budgets.
signals.evidence: He says IT is usually only about 3-7% of corporate revenue, so productivity-driving AI compute will move into marketing, sales, manufacturing, and other operating budgets that lack FinOps tooling.

signals.claim: Levie expects enterprises to use a mosaic of models rather than route every task to the frontier model.
signals.evidence: He says tasks that become reliable can be peeled off to cheaper models, while coding, life sciences, contracts, and financial planning may still justify top-tier models.

signals.claim: Levie says access control is a core reason knowledge-work agents diffuse more slowly than coding agents.
signals.evidence: He says coding agents can often consume the needed codebase, while enterprise agents either lack access, overreach into data they should not use, or create data-leakage blast radius across vendors.

signals.claim: Levie says headless software will create dual seat and consumption models for enterprise SaaS.
signals.evidence: He predicts agents will hit systems far more than humans do, so software vendors will keep seats for human users but charge consumption for agentic access beyond allocation.

signals.claim: Levie remains bullish on vertical AI apps because workflows, data integration, and change management are too specific for labs to own alone.
signals.evidence: He says applied vendors still matter where products compress model output, context, implementation, and user workflow into something knowledge workers can use without managing skills files or prompts.

summary: Aaron Levie gives a dense enterprise-AI readout: token spend has become a top CIO issue, single-task agent runs can reach roughly $1,000, AI spend is moving from IT to business-unit budgets, and enterprises will use multiple models rather than one frontier default. He also argues headless agent access will force SaaS vendors toward dual seat-plus-consumption pricing.
why_it_matters: This is a concrete operating model for enterprise AI adoption. The bottlenecks are no longer generic enthusiasm; they are budget ownership, model routing, access control, FinOps for tokens, SaaS pricing, and the implementation layer between frontier labs and real workflows.
